tier_reason: First-party benchmark code is public (benchmarks/benchmark.js, run via npm run benchmark) and the README screenshot (benchmark.png, refreshed in the last commit on 2019-04-06) shows SuperFastHash (js) 447.736 ms vs (wasm) 369.101 ms per 1,000,000 hashes, but no CPU model, Node version or V8 version is given, so it cannot reach A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript compiler (asc from the GitHub master branch, 2019) with -O3 --validate via buildwasm.js; Node.js version not stated (package.json engines: node >=10.10.0)
corrections.workload: 1,000,000 random messages of 1-1000 bytes (crypto.randomBytes) generated once and hashed once each per implementation by benchmarks/benchmark.js (console.time around Array.forEach, one pass, no warm-up); the README shows the output only as a macOS terminal screenshot (benchmark.png).
corrections.caveats: Numbers exist only in a terminal screenshot in the repo; no CPU, Node version or V8 version stated. Single run per implementation with no warm-up: the JS implementation runs first in the same process, so its timed pass includes JIT tier-up, which favours the Wasm pass that runs second. Wasm timings include copying every message into Wasm linear memory (wasmMemory.set) and the JS-to-Wasm call, so the ~1.21x gain is end-to-end but small enough that run order could account for part of it. The native crypto rows (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, RIPEMD-160) build a Hash object per message and are cryptographic hashes, so they are not like for like. Last commit 2019-04-06.

notes: Numbers match the screenshot exactly; ISC licence, 19 stars, 9 commits, last commit 2019-04-06 (abandoned) all confirmed. Main shortcomings: tiny ~1.21x margin (derived from page data) from a single unwarmed run with JS first, and no hardware or runtime version. The 'listed as unmaintained on awesome-assemblyscript' caveat was not checked (that list's raw README did not resolve).

tier_reason: First-party: README ranges and committed charts (charts/utf-vs-stdlib-*-v8.png) come from the public harness assembly/__benches__/utf-vs-stdlib.bench.ts, built and run by scripts/run-bench.sh with full asc/wasm-opt/d8 flags, but no CPU model is stated for the charts, so it is C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: scripts/run-bench.sh (V8 target): asc -O3 --converge --noAssert --uncheckedBehavior always --runtime incremental --enable bulk-memory --enable simd, then wasm-opt -O4 -tnh -iit -ifwl -s 0 with SIMD, bulk-memory, nontrapping-float-to-int and tail-call enabled (when wasm-opt is installed); run under d8 --no-liftoff; AssemblyScript ^0.28.19
corrections.workload: Public UTF8.decode / UTF8.encode vs AssemblyScript stdlib String.UTF8.decode / encode over 14 simdutf wikipedia_mars HTML payloads plus emoji.txt (assembly/__benches__/utf-vs-stdlib.bench.ts: 200-op batches, warm-up, at least 1 s timed, results passed through blackbox); UTF8.validate and UTF16.validate timed on their own in utf-validate-simdutf.bench.ts and utf16-validate-simdutf.bench.ts.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: UTF8.decode 2.1-6.7x faster than String.UTF8.decode and UTF8.encode 4.3-9.4x faster than String.UTF8.encode on the HTML payloads; UTF8.validate up to 55.4 GB/s on ASCII-heavy HTML (11.9-34.4 GB/s on other HTML); UTF16.validate up to 87 GB/s on surrogate-free HTML. The committed charts show the HTML-only qualifier matters: on emoji.txt UTF8.decode is slower than the stdlib (1.6 vs 2.5 GB/s) and UTF8.encode is level (1.0 vs 1.0 GB/s). Chart labels give english.html decode 17.5 vs 2.5 GB/s (about 7.0x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Baseline is AssemblyScript's own stdlib transcoder, not JavaScript TextEncoder/TextDecoder or a C++/Emscripten build. The speedup ranges cover the 14 HTML payloads only; on emoji.txt the public decode is slower than the stdlib (1.6 vs 2.5 GB/s) and encode shows no gain (1.0 vs 1.0 GB/s). The validate figures have no baseline at all (the stdlib has no validator, and simdutf itself is not run despite the 'simdutf' chart names, which refer to its payload files). The SWAR bars write into preallocated buffers while the stdlib allocates its result, so only the SIMD (public API) bars are like for like. No CPU model is stated for the charts (CHANGELOG 0.1.0 cites V8 on Apple Silicon without a model; a 2026-09-24 commit refreshed ARM64 and AMD64 charts without saying which one the README shows). The kernels are a port of simdutf's westmere SSE4 kernels to 128-bit Wasm SIMD (simdutf is already listed in wave 7). Very new, 1 star.

notes: Claims match the README and the charts it pins (identical to HEAD charts); MIT, 1 star, 32 commits, last commit 2026-09-25 confirmed. Main shortcomings: AS-stdlib-only baseline, no CPU model, emoji.txt decode slower than stdlib, validate numbers without baseline. Orchestrator may want to weigh whether this is a port of simdutf (wave 7) for duplicate handling; its claim is against a different baseline and it adds its own SWAR paths, so I kept it as its own entry.

tier_reason: First-party informal observation in the README (15 characters: about 5-10 FPS with the TypeScript manager vs an easy 60 FPS with the C++/Wasm manager on a third-gen i3); the code and emcc flags are public but there is no timing harness, no exact CPU model and no browser version, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: emcc ./cc/naivewasmanimationmanager.cc -O3 -s SIDE_MODULE=1 -s WASM=1 (makefile), Emscripten sdk-incoming-64bit with binaryen-master (2017); TypeScript ^2.2 bundled with webpack 2; browser and engine version not stated
corrections.caveats: Informal one-machine observation from a 2017 browser/engine generation with no timing harness or FPS log in the repo; 60 FPS is probably vsync-capped so the true gap is unknown. Both managers use the same naive algorithm (per-bone recursive recomputation of the parent chain, binary keyframe search; the Apr 2017 linear-to-binary search fix was applied to both), but the TypeScript side looks bones up by string name in Maps and allocates new Mat4/Vec3/Float32Array objects per bone per frame, while the C++ side uses integer bone IDs and stack temporaries, so part of the gap is data layout and GC pressure rather than the engine. The author calls the logic only 'nearly' identical. MIT licence is in license.md. Listed on awesome-wasm.

notes: README sentence confirmed; 226 stars, 23 forks, MIT (license.md), 26 commits, last commit 2017-04-25 (abandoned). Main shortcomings: anecdotal FPS from one machine, vsync cap hides the real ratio, JS side allocates per frame and uses string-keyed Map lookups.
